sections.h2: City or county: who gets the check
sections.html:
For current-year tax, the City of Kenosha is the payee through July 31. Kenosha County takes over after that date. A payment on a city parcel that lands at the county early gets sent back. The county does accept city-parcel payments for earlier tax years and for balances still delinquent after July 31.

The county treasurer's downtown office is inside the city limits, at 1010 56th Street, Kenosha, WI 53140, phone 262-653-2542. It collects delinquent and prior-year tax on city parcels and runs the tax deed process on parcels that stay unpaid. Each year the treasurer also settles with the school districts, Gateway Technical College and the state revenue department, so a single Kenosha bill carries the levies of several governments.

Owners here can pay in one lump or in three pieces, on January 31, April 30 and July 31. The pattern comes from Wis. Stat. 74.12, which requires any installment ordinance to collect the first piece by January 31, at least half of the total by April 30 and the rest by July 31.

December is when bills should arrive, with the mailing deadline set by 74.09(5) at the month's third Monday. Call the city treasurer to confirm exactly what you owe on each date, because the second and third installments depend on what you paid earlier.

A late installment accelerates the rest of the bill, and interest begins. Miss the first installment and all unpaid tax is delinquent on February 1 (74.12(7)). Miss a later one and the unpaid balance is delinquent the next month's first day (74.12(8)), with interest and penalty counted from the earlier February 1 under 74.12(10).

The interest rate is 1 percent monthly, and by ordinance a county can add as much as 0.5 percent more (74.47). Kenosha County quotes 18 percent a year in all. Late money paid through July 31 goes to the city treasurer; then the city hands its roll to the county by August 15 and the county collects what remains (74.12(10) and (12)).

City residents are told to phone the city treasurer up to July 31 and the County Treasurer afterward. For tax that stays unpaid, the county can arrange a plan clearing each delinquent year within 10 months. Three years of delinquency opens tax deed foreclosure, so a seller with back tax should settle well before that.

The formula starts with assessed value divided by 1,000, times the combined mill rate. Total taxes, less the lottery credit and the first dollar credit, give net property taxes, and special assessments and special charges are added to reach the bill. The county's Property & Taxes page lists current and past county mill rates.

Your bill shows the rate for your parcel and the amount owed to each taxing body, so compare those lines from year to year before assuming the city raised its share.

Wisconsin limits how quickly a local levy can grow, but a bill can still jump. A higher assessment, a new special assessment for a street, sewer or sidewalk, or a voter-approved referendum can each do it. Bills must list recent referendum amounts under 74.09(3)(db).

Call the City Assessor's Office first. If the answer stands, the Board of Review is next. City boards sit in the council chamber or another spot the council chooses (70.47(1)), at some point in the 45 days after the fourth Monday of April. The clerk posts the meeting notice at least 15 days ahead, or 30 days ahead when the city is revaluing.

The rules for appearing are strict:

  • Give the board clerk notice, spoken or written, 48 or more hours before the board first meets.
  • Hand over a written objection on the board's form during the opening two hours of that session.
  • Object to land and buildings together. You cannot contest only one.
  • Let the assessor see the outside of the property if asked. Under 70.47(7)(aa), an owner who refuses a reasonable certified-mail request gives up the right to appear.

A ruling against you starts a 90-day clock from the decision notice for a court action by certiorari (70.47(13)). Reach out to the assessor early next spring to learn when open book is held.

Who owes what for the sale year is a matter for the purchase contract. Where it says nothing, Wis. Stat. 74.15 has the seller repay the buyer for the months before closing, at one-twelfth of last year's tax per month, with the closing month counted when the deed is dated after the 15th. Many Kenosha contracts write their own proration, and in that case the title company's figure controls.

A seller who owes tax should ask the city treasurer, or the County Treasurer after July 31, for a payoff good through closing day. It includes interest and penalty, and an unpaid special assessment or special charge can put the whole parcel into delinquency. A mortgage escrow does not change this, since the owner is still responsible for making sure the lender paid. With a cash buyer the payoff is simply deducted at the closing table.

Some owners also get relief. The Lottery and Gaming Credit is for owners whose primary residence was the home on January 1. The Homestead Credit, claimed with state income tax, helps lower-income owners. Disabled service members can ask the County service office about the state's property tax credit for them.

The city lies on Lake Michigan's southwestern shore, roughly 32 miles south of Milwaukee and 49 miles north of Chicago. At 99,986 people in 2020 it ranked fourth among Wisconsin cities, and the 2025 estimate is 99,239. Metra commuter rail runs to Chicago, and I-94, WIS 50 and WIS 32 are the main roads.

The city has about 40,333 households. Owners live in 58.7 percent of homes, the median home value is $225,200, rent runs a median $1,186 and household income a median $71,239. The former AMC lakefront plant site is now the HarborPark neighborhood, and locals divide the city into Downtown, Uptown and the area west of I-94. Winters can be hard on roofs and gutters, so buyers often ask about their condition.

faqs.q: When are Kenosha, WI property taxes due?
faqs.a: Either all at once or in three installments, January 31, April 30 and July 31. Current-year payments go to the City of Kenosha until July 31, then to the County Treasurer.

faqs.q: Do I pay Kenosha property tax to the city or the county?
faqs.a: Pay the City of Kenosha for current-year tax through July 31. Pay the Kenosha County Treasurer for prior-year tax and for delinquent balances after July 31.

faqs.q: How much interest is charged on late Kenosha property tax?
faqs.a: The rate is 1 percent monthly under Wis. Stat. 74.47, and the county lists interest and penalty together as 18 percent yearly, beginning February 1 after a missed first installment.

faqs.q: Can I sell my Kenosha house if I owe back property tax?
faqs.a: Yes. Ask the treasurer for a payoff figure valid through closing, and the balance gets cleared then. Paying sooner keeps you away from the tax deed process, which starts after three years of delinquency.

faqs.q: How do I contest my Kenosha property assessment?
faqs.a: Speak to the City Assessor's Office. Next, warn the Board of Review clerk 48 hours before the first meeting and file the objection inside its first two hours. Certiorari review in court has to start within 90 days of the decision notice.
